slides.say: Given: x plus four y, in absolute value, is equal to four x plus y, in absolute value. Which of the following is necessarily true?
One equation, two unknowns, and bars on both sides. [short pause] We'll solve it three ways, two cases, squaring both sides, and plugging in numbers.
[short pause] Our first method, two cases. Two absolute values are equal when the insides are equal, or when one is the opposite of the other.
Option one, they're equal. x plus four y is four x plus y. Move the x's to one side and the y's to the other. Three y is three x, so y is x.
Option two, they're opposites. x plus four y is minus, open bracket, four x plus y. That's minus four x minus y.
Move everything to one side, and five x plus five y is zero. So x is minus y.

So x is y, or x is minus y. Number two, x is y, is only half the story, because x could be minus y. But number three, the absolute value of x equals the absolute value of y. Equal or opposite, it's the same size in both cases. Always true. Number three is our answer.
And numbers one and four? When x is y, x isn't smaller than y, and y isn't smaller than x. Out.
[pause] Our second method, squaring both sides. Bars on both sides, and both sides are zero or positive. So I'm allowed to square them, and after squaring, the bars are gone.
Open both with the shortcut formula. On the left, x squared plus eight x y plus sixteen y squared. On the right, sixteen x squared plus eight x y plus y squared.
Eight x y is on both sides, so it cancels. Move the terms, and fifteen y squared is fifteen x squared. Divide by fifteen, and y squared is x squared.
And remember, bars and even powers act alike. If the squares are equal, the absolute values are equal. Number three.

[pause] Our third method, plugging in numbers. It's not so obvious here, but it's the shortest. Look at the given. If x and y are equal, both sides are the same. So x two and y two. Ten on both sides, it works.
at: So x two and y two

slides.say: With equal numbers, y smaller than x is false, and x smaller than y is false. Numbers one and four are out.
at: y smaller than x is false
x smaller than y is false

slides.say: Two and three both survive, and the answers give us a hint. Equal, or equal in absolute value. So the tie-breaker is opposite numbers. x two and y minus two. Two minus eight is minus six, and eight minus two is six. Six and six, it works.
at: x two and y minus two

slides.say: So they don't have to be equal, and number two is out. Number three.
And the mirror test sees part of it with no numbers at all. Swap x and y, and the given doesn't change. So y smaller than x and x smaller than y turn into each other, and both go out.
Three approaches. The third is the hardest to spot, but it's the shortest. Pick what feels comfortable for you. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
